questions.question: Apart from making a business easy to deal with, a good process in the marketing mix also:

options.a: Removes the need to train staff
options.b: Guarantees the business the highest price in the market
options.c: Saves time and money and keeps the standard of service consistent

questions.explanation: An efficient process saves time and money and keeps service quality consistent, which builds brand reputation and customer loyalty. Option A is wrong because staff still need training under the people element, option B overstates what process can do, and option D is wrong because promotion is still needed.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A hotel in Victoria Island sends all its front-desk and customer service staff on a two-week training programme so they serve guests better. Which element of the marketing mix is it strengthening?
questions.explanation: The people element covers those who deliver the marketing and service, and the firm needs staff who are fully trained for the job. Option B is about procedures rather than staff skills, option C is about distribution, and option D is about the offering itself.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Everything a customer sees or hears when interacting with a business, such as its branding, packaging and shop space, is referred to as:
questions.explanation: Physical evidence is the visible and audible side of the business, including branding, packaging, premises and how staff look and behave. Option A is distribution, option B is marketing communication, and option C is the way the service is delivered.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Which of the following is part of a business's physical evidence?

options.b: The way its staff and sales representatives act and dress
options.c: Its physical space, such as a shop

questions.explanation: Physical evidence covers everything customers see or hear when dealing with the business, so it includes branding and packaging, the shop itself and how staff act and dress. Since options A, B and C are all examples, all of the above is correct.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A restaurant in Lekki repaints its dining hall, installs new lighting, reprints its menus and puts up a new signboard. Which element of the services marketing mix is it changing?
questions.explanation: The look of the premises, menus and signboard are things customers see, so they form the restaurant's physical evidence. Option D is about how orders are taken and served, option C is about staff, and option A is about how much is charged.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Which statement about the elements of the marketing mix is correct?

options.a: The elements work together, and they also affect segmentation, targeting and positioning decisions
options.b: Each element should be planned separately without reference to the others
options.c: The mix is fixed once set and never changes over a product's life
options.d: Only the product element affects positioning

questions.explanation: The Ps must work together to make the business successful, and they also shape how the firm segments, targets and positions itself. Option B contradicts this, option D wrongly limits positioning to one element, and option C is wrong because the mix is adjusted as the product moves through its life cycle.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: When the 4Ps are viewed from the customer's point of view as the 4Cs, place corresponds to:
questions.explanation: Seen from the buyer's side, place is about how easy it is to obtain the product, which is convenience. Option A matches promotion, option D matches price, and option B matches product.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: The course of a product's sales and profits over its lifetime is known as the:
questions.explanation: The product life cycle traces how a product's sales and profits change from launch through growth and maturity to decline. Option A is the set of marketing tools, option C is the full range of products a firm sells, and option D is the mental steps an individual goes through in accepting a new product.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Once a product reaches the sales decline phase of its life cycle, marketers need to:

options.a: Return the product to the introduction stage by relaunching it unchanged
options.c: Raise prices to the highest level possible
options.d: Find new ways to increase sales again

questions.explanation: In decline, marketers must look for new ways to lift sales, for example by repositioning, finding new uses, or deciding whether to keep, harvest or drop the product. Option B gives up without analysis, option C would usually speed up the fall in demand, and option A would not change anything customers care about.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A new brand of plantain chips was launched six months ago. Sales are slow, few customers know it, there are almost no direct competitors, and the firm is spending heavily on making people aware of it. The product is in the:
questions.explanation: Slow sales, low awareness, few competitors and heavy awareness spending are signs of the introduction stage. Option B would show rapidly rising sales and new competitors, option D would show high but levelling sales and strong competition, and option A would show falling sales.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A bottled-water brand's yearly sales rose from N10 million to N25 million and then to N60 million over three years, while several new competitors entered the market. The brand is most likely in the:
questions.explanation: Sales more than doubling each year while new competitors are attracted by the opportunity is the classic picture of the growth stage. Option A would show slow sales with few rivals, option B would show sales levelling off, and option C would show sales falling.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: In which stage of the product life cycle do sales typically reach their peak and the stage usually last longer than the others?
questions.explanation: In maturity, sales growth slows and sales peak, and this stage normally lasts longer than the others, so most products on the market are mature. Option A has rising but not yet peak sales, option D has low sales, and option C has falling sales.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: In which stage of the product life cycle is the cost per customer typically highest?
questions.explanation: In the introduction stage, the firm spends heavily on distribution and promotion while only a few customers are buying, so the cost per customer is high. In growth (option D) costs per customer fall to an average level, and in maturity (option B) and decline (option C) they are low.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: The customers who buy a product mainly during its decline stage are usually described as:
questions.explanation: Laggards are the last to adopt and are typically the main buyers left when a product is in decline. Option C buys at introduction, option A buys during growth, and option B makes up the bulk of buyers in maturity.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: 'Use heavy sales promotion to entice trial' and 'build product awareness among early adopters and dealers' are recommended strategies for which stage of the product life cycle?
questions.explanation: At introduction few people know the product, so the firm promotes heavily to get people to try it and to get dealers to stock it. In growth (option D) demand is already strong so sales promotion is reduced, in maturity (option C) promotion encourages brand switching, and in decline (option B) it is cut to a minimum.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A firm's advertising for a well-established detergent now stresses brand differences and benefits, and it increases sales promotion to encourage customers of rival brands to switch. The detergent is in the:
questions.explanation: In maturity, the market is crowded, so firms stress how their brand differs and use promotions to win customers from competitors. Option A focuses on building mass-market awareness while demand rises, option C focuses on getting first trial, and option B cuts promotion to a minimum.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Phasing out weak items, cutting prices, closing unprofitable outlets and reducing advertising to the level needed to keep hard-core loyal customers are strategies for which stage?
questions.explanation: In decline, sales and profits are falling, so the firm trims weak products and outlets and spends only enough to keep its most loyal buyers. Option A defends market share with strong promotion, option B expands distribution and product extensions, and option C invests to build awareness.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A mature brand of tea in Nigeria starts promoting iced tea for hot afternoons to young people who never drank tea before, trying to find new users and new uses. This is an example of:
questions.explanation: Modifying the market means increasing consumption by finding new users, new market segments or new uses for the product. Option D changes the product's features, quality or style, option A is a decline-stage tactic of cutting costs, and option B is a launch pricing strategy.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A noodles brand in decline stops spending on research and advertising and cuts other costs, hoping that sales hold up for a while so that it earns extra cash in the short run. This decline-stage strategy is called:
questions.explanation: Harvesting means reducing costs such as research, advertising and sales force spending while hoping sales hold up, which raises short-run profit. Option A keeps the brand going without change, option C sells it off or withdraws it, and option D is a maturity-stage move to find new users.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: A product that enjoys a short period of unusually high sales driven by consumer enthusiasm and immediate popularity, and then quickly fades, is called a:
questions.explanation: A fad rises quickly, is adopted with great zeal, peaks early and declines very fast. Option D is a basic, distinctive mode of expression that can last for generations, option B is a currently popular style that grows and declines slowly, and option C is a product class, not a life cycle pattern.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: In the services marketing mix, the idea of 'physical evidence' is especially important because services are:

options.a: Usually stored in warehouses before sale
options.c: Produced without the involvement of staff
options.d: Intangible, so customers look for visible cues to judge quality

questions.explanation: Services cannot be seen, touched or tasted before purchase, so customers judge them by what they can see, such as the premises, branding and staff appearance. Option B is not generally true, option A is wrong because services cannot be stored, and option C is wrong because staff are usually central to service delivery.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Empty seats on a Lagos-Abuja flight that departs half full cannot be stored and sold the next day. This characteristic of services is called:
questions.explanation: Perishability means services cannot be stored for later sale or use, so unused capacity is lost. Option B means services cannot be seen or touched before purchase, option C means services are produced and consumed at the same time, and option D means quality depends on who provides the service and when.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: Some customers at a barbing salon in Yaba wait for one particular barber because the quality of a haircut differs from one barber to another. This characteristic of services is called:
questions.explanation: Variability means service quality depends on who provides it, when, where and how, which is why the people and process elements need careful management. Option D means services cannot be stored, option A means they cannot be seen before purchase, and option C means they cannot be separated from their providers.

questions.topic: Marketing Mix and Product Life Cycle
questions.question: In a year when total industry sales of bottled water in a state are N800 million, one brand sells N120 million worth. What is the brand's market share?
questions.explanation: Market share is the firm's sales divided by total industry sales, times 100: 120 / 800 x 100 = 15%. Option C is the share held by all other brands (100 - 15), option D comes from dividing the wrong way round (800 / 120), and option B comes from misplacing the decimal point when converting 0.15 to a percentage.

questions.question: Market segmentation involves:

options.a: Treating all customers in exactly the same way
options.d: Dividing a broad market into smaller groups with shared characteristics

questions.explanation: Market segmentation is the process of dividing a broad market into smaller groups of customers who share meaningful characteristics such as demographics, geography, psychographics or behaviour. Options A and B describe the opposite approach, mass marketing that ignores differences. Option C is not what segmentation means.

questions.question: Which segmentation basis is most sensitive to regional product preferences?
questions.explanation: Geographic segmentation groups customers by where they live or work, such as country, state, city, climate or urban versus rural area, so it directly captures regional differences in what people buy. Option D uses population features such as age and income, option A uses personality and lifestyle, and option B uses buying and usage patterns.

questions.question: Demographic segmentation uses variables like:
questions.explanation: Demographic segmentation groups people by population characteristics such as age, sex, religion, income and occupation. Option B is a psychographic variable, option A is geographic, and option D is a behavioural variable.

questions.question: Psychographic segmentation uncovers:

options.d: Intangible factors such as values and lifestyles

questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation groups people by psychological traits: their values, attitudes, lifestyle, personality and motivations. Option C is the focus of demographic segmentation, option A is geographic, and option B is behavioural segmentation.

questions.question: Behavioural segmentation prioritizes:

options.a: Consumer usage, loyalty and purchase occasions

questions.explanation: Behavioural segmentation groups customers by how they act towards a product: how often they use it, how loyal they are, when they buy and what benefits they seek. Option B is geographic, option D is demographic, and option C is psychographic.

questions.question: The strategic goal of market segmentation is to:

options.d: Meet diverse customer needs more precisely

questions.explanation: Segmentation lets a firm tailor its products and marketing to each group, so it can satisfy different customer needs more precisely and profitably. Option B is the mass-marketing approach that segmentation moves away from. Options A and C are not goals of segmentation.

questions.question: Geographic segmentation is most important when:

options.b: Consumer needs and tastes differ by region

questions.explanation: Geographic segmentation matters most when where people live affects what they buy, for example because of climate, culture, language or how urban an area is. Option D points to demographic segmentation, option A to psychographic segmentation, and option C to behavioural segmentation.

questions.question: Targeting "millennials with disposable income" is an example of:
questions.explanation: Both parts of this target are demographic: millennials is a generation (an age group) and disposable income is an income variable. Option B would focus on lifestyle or personality, option A on location, and option D on buying or usage behaviour.

questions.question: Psychographic segmentation provides insights into:
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation looks at how people think and live, including their motivations, values, attitudes and lifestyles. Option C relates to geographic segmentation, option A is a behavioural variable, and option B belongs to demographic segmentation.

questions.question: Behavioural segmentation might target:
questions.explanation: Brand loyalty is a behaviour, because it describes how customers act towards a brand, so targeting loyal customers is behavioural segmentation. Option A is demographic, option C is geographic, and option B is psychographic because it is based on personality.

questions.question: Market segmentation enables firms to:

options.b: Customize offerings for distinct customer groups

questions.explanation: Once a market is divided into segments, a firm can design products, prices and messages that fit each group's particular needs. Options A, D and C are not benefits of segmentation.

questions.question: Targeting "coastal residents" reflects:
questions.explanation: Coastal residents are defined by where they live, which makes this geographic segmentation. Option B would use age, income or similar population features, option D would use lifestyle or personality, and option C would use buying or usage behaviour.

questions.question: A key strength of demographic segmentation is:

options.a: Its use of measurable, easily available data

questions.explanation: Demographic variables such as age, sex, income and occupation are easy to measure and data on them is widely available, which is why demographic segmentation is the most commonly used type. Option B describes psychographic segmentation, option D describes geographic segmentation, and option C describes behavioural segmentation.

questions.question: Psychographic segmentation includes variables like:
questions.explanation: Attitudes, interests and opinions are psychological variables, so they belong to psychographic segmentation along with values, lifestyle and personality. Option B is demographic, option D is geographic, and option C is behavioural.

questions.question: Behavioural segmentation can segment customers by:

options.b: How heavily they use the product

questions.explanation: Usage rate (light, medium or heavy users) describes how customers behave towards a product, so it is a behavioural variable. Option A is geographic, option C is demographic, and option D is psychographic.

questions.question: Market segmentation improves efficiency by:
questions.explanation: Segmentation helps a firm see which groups are most attractive and focus its money and effort on them instead of spreading resources thinly across everyone. Option C is the mass-marketing approach that wastes effort on people unlikely to buy. Options A and D are not benefits of segmentation.

questions.question: Targeting "frequent flyers" is an example of:
questions.explanation: Frequent flyers are defined by how often they use a service, which is a usage-rate variable, so this is behavioural segmentation. Option C would use location, option B would use features such as age or income, and option D would use lifestyle or personality.

questions.question: Geographic segmentation works best in markets where:

options.b: Regional tastes or climates shape demand

questions.explanation: Geographic segmentation is most useful when location changes what people want, for example when climate, season or local culture affects demand. Option C is a case where location makes little difference to demand. Options A and D say nothing about regional differences.

questions.question: Psychographic segmentation is very useful for:

options.d: Understanding why consumers choose certain brands

questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation looks at motivations, values, attitudes and lifestyle, so it helps explain why people prefer one brand over another. Option A is geographic, option C is behavioural, and option B is demographic.

questions.question: Market segmentation improves marketing by:

options.d: Focusing efforts on solutions tailored to each customer group

questions.explanation: Segmentation helps a firm design products and messages that fit each group's specific needs, which makes its marketing more relevant and effective. Option B describes mass marketing, the opposite of segmentation. Options A and C are not benefits of segmentation.

questions.question: A consumer's activities, interests and opinions (AIO) describe his or her ______, a psychographic variable used in market segmentation.
questions.explanation: Lifestyle is the pattern of how a person lives, measured by his or her activities, interests and opinions, and it is an important psychographic segmentation variable. Option A is a demographic variable, option D is a geographic one, and option C is a behavioural variable based on how much of a product a person uses.

questions.question: Dividing a market into groups based on variables such as age, sex, religion and income is called ______ segmentation.
questions.explanation: Demographic segmentation groups people by population characteristics such as age, sex, religion, income and occupation, and it is the most common form of segmentation. Option B uses psychological traits such as lifestyle, values and personality. Option C uses location, and option A uses how people buy or use the product.

questions.question: Lifestyle, personality, attitudes and values are variables used in ______ segmentation.
questions.explanation: Psychographic segmentation groups customers by their psychological traits: how they live, what they value, their attitudes and their personality. Option D uses measurable population facts such as age and income, and option B uses location. Option A groups buyers by actions such as usage rate or brand loyalty rather than by inner traits.

questions.question: Market segmentation strategy is the opposite of
questions.explanation: Mass marketing treats the whole market as one and offers a single product and marketing mix to everyone, while segmentation divides the market into groups and tailors a mix to each. Option C is selling by telephone, a promotion method rather than a market coverage strategy. Option B deals with smoothing irregular demand over time.

questions.question: Segmentation focuses on the ______, whereas product differentiation focuses on ______.
questions.explanation: Segmentation starts from the market: it groups buyers with similar needs and adjusts the offer to fit each group. Differentiation starts from the product: it stresses how the firm's product differs from rivals' to win buyers. Option B simply reverses the two ideas, and the price-based options do not describe either strategy.

questions.question: When consumer preferences are so scattered that, in the extreme, each consumer could be treated as a separate market segment, the market shows
questions.explanation: Diffused preferences are spread widely with no natural grouping, so at the extreme every buyer differs and could be a segment of one. Option D describes buyers falling into distinct groups that form natural segments. Option C means everyone wants roughly the same thing, so the whole market is one segment.

questions.question: Which preference pattern exists when groups of consumers with similar preferences form distinct market segments?
questions.explanation: Clustered preferences occur when buyers bunch into distinct groups, each with its own shared preference, so each cluster becomes a natural segment. Option A means all consumers want roughly the same thing, giving one segment. Option B means preferences are scattered with no clear groups.

questions.question: Which preference pattern allows all consumers to be treated as a single market segment?
questions.explanation: Homogeneous preferences mean consumers want roughly the same thing, so the whole market can be served as one segment with one offer. Option B gives several natural groups, each a separate segment. Option D means preferences are widely scattered.

questions.question: In which of these markets are consumer preferences most likely to be homogeneous?
questions.explanation: Table salt is a basic product that most buyers want in much the same form, so preferences are fairly uniform or homogeneous. Fashion clothing (option A), perfume (option D) and cars (option C) attract widely different tastes in style, scent, size and price, so their preferences are far more varied.

questions.question: In benefit segmentation, market segments are identified according to

options.a: the age and income of consumers
options.b: what consumers want from the product
options.d: how often consumers buy the product

questions.explanation: Benefit segmentation groups buyers by the benefits they seek, that is, what they want the product to do for them, such as whiteness or decay protection from toothpaste. Option A describes demographic segmentation by consumer characteristics. Option D is a behavioural basis based on usage rate.

questions.question: ______ focuses on what consumers do, such as how often they buy and how they use the product.
questions.explanation: Behavioural segmentation groups buyers by their actions, such as purchase occasion, usage rate, loyalty and how they use the product. Option A focuses on what consumers want rather than what they do. Option D uses who consumers are, such as age, sex and income.

questions.question: Which approach uses demographic variables such as age, sex and income to segment markets?
questions.explanation: Segmentation by consumer characteristics describes who the buyers are, using demographic variables like age, sex, income and occupation. Option C uses personality, lifestyle and attitudes instead. Option A groups buyers by what they do with the product.

questions.question: The following are major requirements for effective segmentation EXCEPT:
questions.explanation: Useful segments should be measurable, substantial, accessible and actionable, so that the firm can size them, profit from them, reach them and serve them. "Ability" is not one of these requirements. Options D, B and A are all standard tests of a good segment.

questions.question: ______ is the degree to which the size and purchasing power of the segments can be measured.
questions.explanation: Measurability asks whether a segment's size and buying power can actually be measured, since a firm cannot plan for a group it cannot size. Option C is about whether the segment is large or profitable enough. Option B is about whether the segment can be reached and served.

questions.question: ______ is the degree to which the segments are large and/or profitable enough to serve.
questions.explanation: Substantiality means the segment is big or profitable enough to justify a separate marketing programme. Option D is about whether its size and buying power can be measured at all. Option C is about whether the firm can design programmes to attract and serve it.

questions.question: ______ is the degree to which the segment can be effectively reached and served.
questions.explanation: Accessibility means the firm can actually reach the segment through suitable media and distribution channels and serve it. Option D is close but refers to being able to design effective programmes for the segment. Option C is about size and profitability.

questions.question: ______ is the degree to which effective programmes can be formulated for attracting and serving the segments.
questions.explanation: Actionability asks whether the firm has the resources to design effective marketing programmes that attract and serve the segment. Option B is about whether the segment can be reached through media and channels. Option C is about sizing the segment.

questions.question: Segmentation bases that use dimensions which simply define or describe the consumers in a segment, such as age, income and location, are called
questions.explanation: Descriptive bases tell us who the consumers in a segment are, using features like demographics and geography. Option B uses dimensions that explain why customers respond to a marketing mix, such as benefits sought. Options D and C are examples of such explanatory or behavioural variables, not descriptions of who the consumer is.

questions.question: Segmentation bases that use dimensions explaining WHY customers respond to marketing mixes, such as the benefits they seek, are called
questions.explanation: Causal bases look for the reasons behind buyers' responses, such as the benefits they seek, so they explain why a segment behaves as it does. Option C only describes who is in the segment. Options B and A are descriptive variables, not causes.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of effective market segmentation?

options.a: Using one identical marketing mix for every customer

questions.explanation: Segmentation exists precisely so a firm does not have to offer one identical mix to everyone; it tailors a mix to each group. By doing so it directs resources to the most promising groups (option B), satisfies customers better (option C) and reveals unmet needs (option D), which can raise sales and profits.

questions.question: The process of dividing a broad market into smaller groups of customers who share meaningful characteristics such as demographics, geography, psychographics or behaviour is called:
questions.explanation: Market segmentation splits a large, mixed market into smaller groups of similar customers so the firm can tailor its offers to each group. Option C is about creating a distinct image in customers' minds, option D is choosing which segments to serve after segmenting, and option A is the set of tools (4Ps) used to serve a market.

questions.question: One of the major reasons marketers segment a market is that segmentation allows them to:

options.a: Serve every customer in the country with one standard product
options.c: Create a custom marketing mix for each segment and cater to it accordingly
options.d: Use exactly the same marketing message for every customer

questions.explanation: Because each segment has shared needs, the firm can design a marketing mix that fits that segment, which makes its marketing more relevant and profitable. Options D and A describe mass marketing, the opposite of segmentation, and option B is wrong because segmentation actually requires research.

questions.question: Which type of market segmentation is described as the most common type, the one most people think of when they hear the term 'market segmentation'?
questions.explanation: Demographic segmentation, using variables such as age, sex, religion and income, is the most widely used form because the data are easy to obtain. Behavioural segmentation (option C) is reported to be the most effective, which is a different claim from being the most common; options A and B are also used but less commonly.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a demographic segmentation variable?
questions.explanation: Personality is a psychological trait, so it is a psychographic variable. Religion (option C), family size (option A) and occupation (option D) describe the population itself and are demographic variables.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the variables examined under psychographic segmentation?
questions.explanation: Time zone is a geographic variable, because it depends on where a customer is located. Inner beliefs (option D), priorities and motivations (option B) and likes and dislikes (option C) are psychographic variables, together with lifestyle, attitudes and values, and personality.

questions.question: An events company advertises the same concert in two ways: to one group it stresses the freedom to choose quiet activities they are comfortable with, and to another it stresses meeting people and socialising. The company is segmenting by:
questions.explanation: Personality segmentation groups people by traits such as being introverted or extroverted, which affect how they respond to an offer. Option B is about how highly society views a person, option A is about how urban an area is, and option C is about whether someone is a current, ex- or potential user.

questions.question: An online sneaker store in Lagos runs one campaign for buyers who want sneakers for jogging and gym work, and a different campaign for buyers who want sneakers as a fashion statement. This is segmentation by:
questions.explanation: Lifestyle segmentation groups customers by the kind of lives they lead, and products are marketed as enhancing that lifestyle, whether active or fashion-focused. Option A is a geographic variable, option D is about social class, and option B is about the words and slang used in a region.

questions.question: A five-star hotel in Abuja advertises luxury experiences and quality service, while a budget hotel in the same city advertises how affordable its rooms are. Each hotel is targeting customers on the basis of:
questions.explanation: Social status is how highly a person is viewed in society, and it shapes buying: upper-class customers respond to luxury, while middle and lower classes care more about affordability. Option A is about traits such as introversion, option B is about how urban an area is, and option D is a behavioural variable about how customers engage with a brand.

questions.question: In psychographic segmentation, people's perceptions of the world, usually shaped by their upbringing and their cultural and religious backgrounds, are called their:
questions.explanation: Attitudes are how people see the world, formed by upbringing, culture and religion, and customers can be grouped by them even though each person's worldview is unique. Option A is the kind of life a person leads, option C is a set of personal traits such as being sociable or creative, and option D is how highly society regards a person.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the six variables of geographic segmentation?
questions.explanation: Spending habits is a behavioural variable, because it describes what customers do rather than where they are. Urbanicity (option D), cultural preferences (option C) and time zone (option B) are geographic variables, along with location, climate and season, and language.

questions.question: Under geographic segmentation, the 'location' variable categorises customers:

options.a: By the climate and season they experience
options.b: Solely by where they live or work, without considering language or culture
options.c: By the slang and colloquialisms they use
options.d: By how urban or rural their area is

questions.explanation: Location looks only at where the customer lives or works and ignores other location-related factors like language or culture. Option D describes urbanicity, option C describes the language variable, and option A describes climate and season, each of which is a separate geographic variable.

questions.question: A clothing retailer promotes raincoats and umbrellas to customers in Port Harcourt during the rainy season, and heavier wear to customers in Jos during the cold harmattan months. Which geographic variable is it using?
questions.explanation: Different regions have different climates and experience seasons at different times, so firms target them with products relevant to that period. Option A groups areas as urban, suburban or rural, option B concerns the words used in each region, and option C concerns cultural norms.

questions.question: A beer brand advertises openly in Lagos but uses very different, more careful marketing in parts of Northern Nigeria where drinking in public may be frowned upon. This is segmentation by:
questions.explanation: Regions differ in culture, and culture strongly affects buying, so firms tailor marketing to each region and avoid what could be offensive there. Options A and B are other geographic variables unrelated to cultural norms, and option D is a behavioural variable about what customers want from the product.

questions.question: A vehicle dealer promotes small saloon cars in city areas, but promotes pick-up trucks that can handle rough roads and haul farm inputs in rural areas. Which geographic variable is it using?
questions.explanation: Urbanicity groups areas by how urban they are, such as urban, suburban and rural, because needs differ; rural buyers may need trucks for rough terrain and farm work. Options C and B are other geographic variables not related to how built-up an area is, and option D is a psychographic variable.

questions.question: A survey of marketers found that 91% of them consider one segmentation method the most effective for their businesses. Which method is it?
questions.explanation: Behavioural segmentation is rated the most effective method because it is based on what customers actually do. Option B is the most common type, which is a different claim from being the most effective, and options A and C were not the method rated most effective.

questions.question: Which of the following is a behavioural segmentation variable?
questions.explanation: Customer journey stage is one of the behavioural variables, along with spending habits, purchasing habits, brand interactions, user status and benefits sought. Options B and C are geographic variables, and option A is a psychographic variable.

questions.question: When customers are grouped by purchasing habits, those who are loyal to their brand and are unlikely to switch to other options are called:
questions.explanation: Habitual buyers stick with their brand and rarely switch, so marketing to them focuses on keeping them. Option B likes its brand but is open to trying others, option A is still researching which product or brand to buy, and option D is happy with its brand but thinks others could offer more.

questions.question: Ada wants to buy her first laptop but does not yet know which brand or model to buy, so she is reading reviews and asking friends to learn about the options. In terms of purchasing habits, she is a:
questions.explanation: Complex buyers do not yet know which product or brand to buy and are still researching the options. Option B is loyal to one brand, option C already has a brand it is happy with but likes trying others, and option A is a usage-rate category, not a purchasing-habit group.

questions.question: Customers can be divided into four groups based on their purchasing habits. Which of the following is NOT one of these four groups?
questions.explanation: The four purchasing-habit groups are complex, variety-seeking, dissonance-reducing and habitual buyers; impulse buying is not one of them. Options B, C and D are all in the list.

questions.question: Generational and life stage segmentation can be regarded as a subset of which type of segmentation?
questions.explanation: Generational and life stage segmentation group customers by age and where they are in life, which are population characteristics, so they fall under demographic segmentation. Option A is about place, option C about actions towards the product, and option B about psychological traits.

questions.question: A social media app markets itself mainly to Generation Z rather than to Generation X, because people born in the same period tend to share characteristics that affect their buying. This is:
questions.explanation: Generational segmentation groups customers by the period in which they were born, such as Generation Z, millennials, Generation X and baby boomers. Option A groups people by current circumstances such as marriage or children, option C groups by location, and option D groups by actions towards the product.

questions.question: Two 30-year-old men grew up in the same Ibadan neighbourhood. One is married with a child; the other is single and still lives with his parents. A marketer who treats them as different segments because of these circumstances is using:
questions.explanation: Life stage segmentation groups people by where they are in life at the moment, such as marriage, children, income and home ownership, so people of the same age can have different needs. Option A would group these two men together because they were born in the same period, option D would also group them together by location, and option C is based on how much of a product people use.

questions.question: When segmenting by income, marketers usually divide the market into:

options.c: High income, mid income and low income groups

questions.explanation: Income decides purchasing power, so marketers commonly split the market into high, mid and low income groups, adjusted to the product and area. Option D is a usage-rate split, option A is an urbanicity split, and option B is a loyalty split.

questions.question: Income is an important segmentation base because it decides a target audience's purchasing power and also helps the marketer decide:

options.a: Whether customers are introverted or extroverted
options.b: Whether to market the product as a need, a want or a luxury
options.c: Which time zone to advertise in
options.d: Which language to use in advertisements

questions.explanation: Income determines what customers can afford, so the same product may be presented as a need to one income group and as a luxury to another. Options C and D are geographic considerations, and option A is a personality (psychographic) consideration.

questions.question: A product that is a necessity for a self-employed trader in Onitsha may be seen as a luxury by a civil servant earning a fixed salary. A marketer who segments on this basis is using:
questions.explanation: Occupation, like income, influences what people see as a need or a luxury, and some products serve only people in particular jobs. Option B groups by male and female, option C by heavy, medium or light use, and option A by weather patterns in a region.

questions.question: A telecoms company groups its market into ex-users, potential users, first-time users and current users of its data plans, and sends each group a different offer. This is segmentation by:
questions.explanation: User status segmentation groups people by their relationship with the product: non-users, ex-users, potential users, first-time users and regular users. Option C groups by what customers want from the product, option A by how urban their area is, and option B by circumstances such as marriage or children.

questions.question: Under behavioural segmentation, labelling customers as brand loyal, brand-neutral or competitor loyal is segmentation by:
questions.explanation: Loyalty segmentation groups customers by how attached they are to a brand: loyal to it, neutral, or loyal to a competitor. Option C is about how much of the product people use, option D is a psychographic variable, and option B is about where a customer is in the buying process.

questions.question: A good market segment is always:
questions.explanation: Members inside a segment should be similar to one another (homogeneous), while different segments should be clearly different from one another (heterogeneous). Option C reverses the two, option D would make segments indistinguishable, and option A would mean members of a segment have nothing in common.

questions.question: Apart from sharing similar features, the members of a market segment must also:

options.c: Respond in a similar way to the marketing activities aimed at them

questions.explanation: Similar characteristics are not enough; members of a segment must react in a similar way to the marketing stimulus so one marketing programme works for all of them. Options A, B and D are far too strict and are not required for a segment to be useful.

questions.question: A skincare company sells an anti-ageing range aimed at mature adults and a separate clear-skin range aimed at teenagers and young adults. The main segmentation base it is using is:
questions.explanation: Offering different ranges to mature adults and to teens and young adults is segmentation by age group, a demographic base common in beauty products. Option D and option C are geographic bases, and option B groups people by the jobs they do.

questions.question: A snack brand sells a large N4,500 party pack in cities where teenagers buy snacks for parties, and small N200 packs in rural areas where people spend little on snacks. This is mainly an example of:
questions.explanation: The brand changes its packs according to where customers live, cities versus the countryside, which is geographic segmentation. Option D would be based on personality or lifestyle, option B on the period people were born, and option C on whether people are new, current or ex-users.

questions.question: After segmenting the Lagos food market, a start-up discovers that no firm is serving healthy, ready-to-eat lunches for night-shift workers, and it launches a service for them. Which benefit of market segmentation does this show?

options.c: Identification of gaps in the market

questions.explanation: Segmentation can reveal groups that are not being served well, opening opportunities a firm can exploit for profit. Option B is about keeping existing customers, option A is about earning more from marketing spending, while option D is related but describes serving known segments better rather than finding an unserved one.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a benefit of market segmentation?

options.a: It removes the need for market research

questions.explanation: Segmentation actually requires extensive research, which is one of its main disadvantages, so it does not remove the need for it. Better matching of needs (option B), increased market share (option C) and customer retention (option D) are all listed benefits.

questions.question: Which of the following is a disadvantage of market segmentation?

options.a: It is an expensive process in terms of both time and money
options.b: It reduces the firm's ability to personalise messages
options.c: It always lowers the firm's market share
options.d: It makes it harder to match customer needs

questions.explanation: Segmentation is costly, because identifying groups and marketing to each differently takes a lot of time and money, and it needs extensive research. Options D and B are the opposite of what segmentation does, and option C contradicts the benefit of increased market share.

questions.question: For market segments to be useful, they should be measurable, accessible, substantial, differentiable and actionable. Which of the following is NOT one of these requirements?
questions.explanation: The five requirements for effective segmentation are measurable, accessible, substantial, differentiable and actionable; being cheap to serve is not one of them. Options B, C and D are all requirements.

questions.question: A firm finds a segment of left-handed golfers in Owerri, but the group is so small that serving it would never be profitable. Which requirement for effective segmentation does this segment fail?
questions.explanation: A substantial segment is large or profitable enough to be worth pursuing with its own marketing programme. Option D is about being able to measure the segment's size and buying power, option B about being able to reach and serve it, and option A about it responding differently from other segments.

questions.question: A marketer identifies a segment that is large and profitable, but its members cannot be reached through any media or distribution channel the firm can use. Which requirement does the segment fail?
questions.explanation: An accessible segment can be effectively reached and served. This one is big enough, so option B is met; option A concerns whether the firm can design programmes to attract the segment, and option D concerns whether its size and purchasing power can be measured.

questions.question: When segments are conceptually distinguishable and respond differently to different marketing mix elements and programmes, they are said to be:
questions.explanation: Differentiable segments react differently to marketing programmes; if two groups respond the same way to every offer, they are not really separate segments. Option A is about reaching the segment, option D about its size and profitability, and option C about the firm's ability to design programmes for it.

questions.question: A small airline identifies seven attractive segments, but its staff and budget are too small to develop separate marketing programmes for each. Which requirement for effective segmentation is lacking?
questions.explanation: Actionable means effective programmes can be designed to attract and serve the segments; a firm without the resources to do so cannot act on them. Option B is about measuring segment size, option A about segments responding differently, and option C about segments being large enough.

questions.question: A target market is best defined as:

options.a: Every person in a country who has money to spend
options.b: A set of buyers sharing common needs or characteristics that a company decides to serve
options.c: The firm's competitors in a particular region
options.d: The place where a product is physically sold

questions.explanation: After segmenting, the firm evaluates the segments and chooses one or more to serve; those chosen buyers are its target market. Option A is the whole population, not a chosen group, option C confuses customers with competitors, and option D describes a retail outlet.

questions.question: A salt producer sells one product with one marketing programme to the whole Nigerian market, ignoring differences between segments. This targeting strategy is:
questions.explanation: Undifferentiated marketing treats the market as one and offers a single product and programme that appeals to what customers have in common. Option D targets several segments with separate offers, option C goes after a large share of one or a few small segments, and option A tailors offers to specific locations or individuals.

questions.question: A drinks company offers a low-sugar drink for health-conscious adults, an energy drink for students and a malt drink for families, each with its own advertising. This targeting strategy is:
questions.explanation: Differentiated marketing targets several segments and designs a separate offer for each. Option A uses one offer for everyone, option C focuses on one or a few small segments, and option B tailors products to single customers.

questions.question: A small Lagos firm with limited resources makes only handmade shoes for people with very large feet, aiming to win a large share of this one small segment. This targeting strategy is:
questions.explanation: Concentrated marketing goes after a large share of one or a few small segments or niches, which suits firms with limited resources. Option A serves many segments with separate offers, option C serves the whole market with one offer, and option D tailors offers to a city or neighbourhood.

questions.question: Tailoring products and marketing programmes to the needs and wants of specific individuals and local customer groups is called:
questions.explanation: Micromarketing, which includes local marketing and individual marketing, is the narrowest targeting strategy. Options A and B are the broadest, treating the whole market as one, and option D is about the image a product holds in customers' minds rather than whom it is tailored to.

questions.question: A tailor in Abeokuta takes each customer's measurements and preferences and makes every outfit to that one customer's order. This is the form of micromarketing called:
questions.explanation: Individual marketing, also called one-to-one marketing, tailors the product and programme to the needs of single customers. Option C tailors offers to cities, neighbourhoods or stores, option B targets one small segment rather than one person, and option D offers one product to everyone.

questions.question: Which option gives the correct order of the main steps in designing a customer-driven marketing strategy?
questions.explanation: A firm first divides the market into segments, then chooses which segments to target, and finally positions its offer in the minds of the chosen customers. Options A, B and C each place a step before the one it depends on.

questions.question: Arranging for a product to occupy a clear, distinctive and desirable place relative to competing products in the minds of target consumers is called:
questions.explanation: Positioning is about how the target customers see the brand compared with competitors. Option C divides the market into groups, option D chooses which groups to serve, and option B is a targeting strategy that serves several segments with different offers.

questions.question: Which of the following segmentation variables is typically used for business (industrial) markets rather than for individual consumers?
questions.explanation: Business buyers can be segmented by industry, company size, location, operating variables, purchasing approaches and similar factors. Options A, C and D describe individual people and are used mainly for consumer markets.

questions.question: A study finds 200,000 potential buyers of a new study app in a city, of whom 35% are aged 16-24. What is the size of the 16-24 segment?
questions.explanation: Segment size is the total market multiplied by the segment's share: 200,000 x 0.35 = 70,000 buyers. Option B is the size of everyone outside the segment (65%), option A misplaces the decimal point, and option D comes from dividing 200,000 by 3.5 instead of multiplying.

questions.question: Out of 300,000 sachet-water units sold in a town in a month, one brand sells 45,000 units. What is the brand's market share for the month?
questions.explanation: Market share is the brand's sales divided by total market sales, times 100: 45,000 / 300,000 x 100 = 15%. Option C is the share of all other brands, option D divides the wrong way round (300,000 / 45,000), and option B wrongly treats the 45,000 figure as a percentage.

questions.question: The simplest marketing system consists of two interacting elements, namely

options.a: the marketing organisation and its target market
options.b: channel members and the marketing organisation
options.c: the marketing organisation and the marketing mix elements
options.d: the target market and channel members

questions.explanation: At its simplest, a marketing system links the marketing organisation and its target market through two flows: products go to customers in exchange for payment, and information flows both ways through selling, advertising and customer feedback. Option C pairs the organisation with tools it controls, not with another party it interacts with. Options D and B bring in channel members, which belong to the larger system but are not part of the simplest two-element one.

questions.question: A set of interacting and interdependent individuals and institutions (producers, suppliers, intermediaries and customers) linked together by flows of goods, money and information is best described as a
questions.explanation: A marketing system is the whole network of participants that are tied together by flows of products, payments and information so that exchange can take place. Option B is the set of controllable tools (such as the 4 Ps) a firm uses, not the network of participants. Option D is a group of similar customers, and Option A is a business philosophy.

questions.question: Which of the following best describes a marketing system?

options.a: The uncontrollable forces outside the firm that affect its decisions
options.b: The set of controllable variables a firm blends to satisfy its target market
options.c: The process of dividing a market into distinct groups of buyers
options.d: The network of firms, suppliers, intermediaries and customers linked by flows of goods, money and information

questions.explanation: A marketing system covers all the parties involved in exchange and the flows that connect them. Option B describes the marketing mix, Option C describes market segmentation, and Option A describes the macro environment, which is only one part of the bigger system.

questions.question: In a simple marketing system, which of the following flows from the seller to the buyer (the market)?
questions.explanation: In the simple model, sellers send goods/services and communication (such as advertising) to the market, while buyers send back money and information. Option B is what moves from buyers to sellers. Option D and Option C wrongly put payment flows going towards the buyer.

questions.question: A pepper seller at a village market in Ogun State sells her own produce directly to shoppers, who pay her in cash and tell her which peppers they prefer. This arrangement is best described as a
questions.explanation: A simple marketing system involves a direct exchange between a seller and buyers, with goods going one way and money and information coming back. Option D involves many interconnected markets, intermediaries and government. Option C and Option A are channel arrangements involving several cooperating firms, which is not the case here.

questions.question: Which of the following correctly distinguishes a complex (modern) marketing system from a simple one?

options.a: The complex system involves only direct sales from producers to final consumers
options.b: The complex system links many markets, such as resource, manufacturer, intermediary, consumer and government markets, rather than just one seller and its buyers
options.c: The complex system excludes the government because it does not buy or sell
options.d: The complex system has no flow of information between buyers and sellers

questions.explanation: In a modern economy, producers buy from resource markets, sell through intermediary markets to consumers, and deal with government, all linked by flows of goods, money and information. Option D is wrong because information still flows. Option A describes a simple system, and Option C is wrong because government buys goods, collects taxes and provides services within the system.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the markets linked together in the structure of a modern exchange economy?
questions.explanation: A modern marketing system links resource markets, manufacturer markets, intermediary markets, consumer markets and government markets. There is no such thing as a marketing mix market; the marketing mix is a set of tools, not a market. Option B, Option A and Option D are all genuine parts of the structure.

questions.question: In the flows of a modern exchange economy, which of the following best describes the role of government markets?

options.a: They supply only raw materials to manufacturers
options.b: They buy goods from other markets, collect taxes and provide public services in return
options.c: They stand completely outside the marketing system
options.d: They act only as retailers selling goods to households

questions.explanation: Governments buy goods from resource, manufacturer and intermediary markets, pay them, collect taxes from these markets and from consumers, and provide services. Option A describes resource markets, and Option D describes intermediaries. Option C is wrong because government is a key participant in the modern system.

questions.question: In a marketing system, in which direction does information mainly flow?

options.c: In both directions, from sellers to buyers and from buyers to sellers

questions.explanation: Sellers communicate with buyers through promotion, while buyers send information back through orders, feedback and market research. Option A describes communication only, and Option B describes feedback only. Option D is far too narrow, since all participants exchange information.

questions.question: In a typical marketing channel, ownership (title) of goods and the physical goods themselves mainly flow

options.a: forward, from the producer towards the final consumer
options.b: backward, from the consumer towards the producer
options.c: only from banks to the producer

questions.explanation: Products and ownership move forward through the channel from producer to wholesaler to retailer to consumer. Payment is the flow that moves backward, so Option B is wrong. Option D and Option C do not describe channel flows of goods or title at all.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT usually regarded as a component of a firm's marketing system?

options.d: The firm's internal accounting depreciation method

questions.explanation: The main components of a marketing system are the firm itself, its suppliers, intermediaries, customers, competitors and the wider environment, linked by flows of goods, money and information. A depreciation method is an internal accounting choice, not a participant in the system. Option B, Option A and Option C are all genuine components.

questions.question: Within the marketing system, the firms that provide the raw materials and other inputs a company needs to produce its goods and services are called
questions.explanation: Suppliers provide the raw inputs and inputs, and the price of these inputs affects the final price of the product. Option C buy finished products and sell them on, Option B offer similar products to the same buyers, and Option D buy the product for final consumption.

questions.question: Firms that help a company establish a link with its customers by promoting, selling and distributing its products are known as
questions.explanation: Marketing intermediaries stand between the firm and its customers and help with promotion, selling and distribution. Option C provide inputs rather than access to customers, Option A fight for the same buyers, and Option B are groups with an interest in the firm rather than channel partners.

questions.question: A beverage company in Ibadan rents space in a warehouse near the Lagos-Ibadan expressway to store its drinks before they are moved to dealers. The warehouse operator is acting as a
questions.explanation: A distribution centre helps organisations store goods, and a warehouse is the standard example. The warehouse does not buy and resell the drinks, so Option B is wrong. Option A would promote the drinks, and Option C would provide finance.

questions.question: An advertising agency that designs a radio campaign to make customers aware of the benefits of a new detergent is an example of which type of marketing intermediary?
questions.explanation: Marketing agencies promote a firm's products by making customers aware of their benefits, and an advertising agency is the typical example. Option C buys and sells the goods, Option D stores them, and Option B finances transactions.

questions.question: Within the micro environment, which components make up the supply side of the firm's marketing system?
questions.explanation: The micro environment is divided into a supply side, made up of suppliers, marketing intermediaries and competitors, and a demand side, made up of customers. Option A is the demand side. Option B wrongly includes government, and Option C are macro environment forces.

questions.question: Two Nigerian noodle brands sell similar products to the same students and each tries to differentiate its packs and flavours to win a bigger share of the market. In the marketing system, each brand is the other's
questions.explanation: Competitors are organisations offering similar products and trying to gain market share through different marketing strategies, which pushes each firm to differentiate. Option D provides inputs, Option A buys to resell, and Option B provides finance; none describes a rival brand.

questions.question: Which of the following best expresses the 'systems' idea behind the marketing system?

options.a: Only the firm matters; suppliers and intermediaries are irrelevant
options.b: The system is fixed and does not change over time
options.c: Its parts are interdependent, so a change in one part (for example, a supplier's price) affects the other parts
options.d: Each participant operates in isolation, so changes in one part have no effect on others

questions.explanation: A system is a set of interacting, interdependent parts, so a change in one component spreads to others, for instance higher input prices leading to higher retail prices and lower demand. Option D and Option A deny this interdependence, and Option B ignores the constant change in the environment.

questions.question: A set of interdependent organisations that help make a product or service available for use or consumption by the consumer or business user is called a
questions.explanation: A marketing channel, also called a distribution channel, is the chain of interdependent organisations, such as wholesalers and retailers, that moves a product to the user. Option A is a group of buyers, Option B refers to inputs coming into the firm, and Option C is the set of communication tools.

questions.question: A Kano farmer sells yoghurt directly to consumers from his farm gate with no wholesaler or retailer involved. This is an example of a
questions.explanation: A zero-level or direct channel has no intermediary levels: the producer sells straight to the final consumer. Option C would include one intermediary such as a retailer, Option D would include a wholesaler and a retailer, and Option A would add a further level such as a jobber or agent.

questions.question: A Nigerian soap manufacturer sells to distributors (wholesalers), who sell to neighbourhood shops (retailers), who then sell to households. How many intermediary levels does this channel have?
questions.explanation: Channel length is counted by the number of intermediary levels between producer and consumer, so wholesaler plus retailer makes a two-level channel. Option C would have only the retailer, Option D would need a third intermediary, and Option A would mean no intermediaries at all.

questions.question: Four textile producers each want to sell to the same five clothing shops. If each producer deals directly with every shop, how many contacts are needed, and how many are needed if all of them deal through one wholesaler instead?

options.a: 29 contacts directly; 9 contacts through the wholesaler
options.b: 9 contacts directly; 20 contacts through the wholesaler
options.c: 20 contacts directly; 9 contacts through the wholesaler
options.d: 20 contacts directly; 20 contacts through the wholesaler

questions.explanation: Without an intermediary, contacts = producers x customers = 4 x 5 = 20. With one wholesaler, each producer and each shop deals only with the wholesaler, so contacts = 4 + 5 = 9. Option B swaps the two results, and Option D wrongly assumes the intermediary saves nothing; reducing the number of contacts is one of the main ways intermediaries add value.

questions.question: Six pharmaceutical producers sell to eight pharmacies in a town. By how many does the number of contacts fall if all trade passes through a single distributor instead of each producer dealing directly with each pharmacy?
questions.explanation: Direct contacts = 6 x 8 = 48; through one distributor contacts = 6 + 8 = 14. The reduction is 48 - 14 = 34. Option B is only the direct total and Option A is only the total through the distributor, so both forget to take the difference.

questions.question: Bringing a product to customers at the right location, at the right time and in a form they can own is how intermediaries in a marketing system mainly create
questions.explanation: Distribution through the marketing system creates place utility (product where buyers are), time utility (available when wanted) and possession utility (transfer of ownership). Option A is created mainly by production, which changes raw inputs into finished goods. Option D and Option C are not utilities created by moving goods.

questions.question: The channel function of shaping and fitting the offer to the buyer's needs, including activities such as manufacturing, grading, assembling and packaging, is called
questions.explanation: Matching means shaping and fitting the offer to the buyer's needs through activities such as grading, assembling and packaging. Option D is reaching agreement on price and terms so ownership can pass, Option A is getting and using funds to cover channel costs, and Option C is bearing the risks of carrying out channel work.

questions.question: A Lagos wholesaler buys 5,000 cartons of tomato paste in advance and stores them, accepting that it will lose money if prices fall or the goods expire before they are sold. Which channel function is the wholesaler performing?
questions.explanation: Risk taking means bearing the risks of carrying out channel work, such as price falls, damage or expiry of stock held. Option A is spreading persuasive communication, Option C is finding and communicating with prospective buyers, and Option D is fitting the offer to buyers' needs.

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT one of the key functions performed by members of a marketing channel?
questions.explanation: Channel members perform functions such as information, promotion, contact, matching, negotiation, physical distribution, financing and risk taking. Setting the national interest rate is done by the central bank as part of the economic environment, not by channel members. Option C, Option B and Option A are genuine channel functions.

questions.question: A channel structure in which producers, wholesalers and retailers act as a unified system, with one member owning the others, having contracts with them or having enough power to make them cooperate, is called a
questions.explanation: A vertical marketing system (VMS) unifies channel levels under ownership, contracts or the power of a channel leader. Option B consists of independent members each seeking its own profit, Option D joins firms at the same level, and Option A is a direct seller-buyer exchange.

questions.question: A manufacturer that joins with dealers through formal franchise agreements, rather than owning them, has created which type of vertical marketing system?
questions.explanation: A contractual VMS links independent firms at different levels through contracts, and franchising is its most common form. Option C combines levels under single ownership, Option B relies on the size and power of one member rather than ownership or contract, and Option D joins firms at the same level.

questions.question: A large Nigerian food company owns its own flour mills, delivery trucks and retail outlets, so it controls production and distribution under a single ownership. This is an example of a
questions.explanation: A corporate VMS integrates successive stages of production and distribution under single ownership. Option B would rely on contracts such as franchises, Option D on the leadership power of a dominant member, and Option C on independent members with no unified control.

questions.question: When two or more companies at the same channel level join together to follow a new marketing opportunity, for example a bank and a supermarket chain agreeing to place bank kiosks inside the supermarkets, the arrangement is called a
questions.explanation: A horizontal marketing system is formed when firms at the same level combine resources to exploit an opportunity. Option C links different levels of the same channel, Option B refers to direct selling, and Option A is a basic seller-buyer exchange.

questions.question: A phone accessories brand sells through its own website, through market traders in Computer Village and through supermarkets at the same time. This use of several channels to reach different customer segments is called
questions.explanation: A multichannel or hybrid distribution system uses two or more marketing channels to reach one or more customer segments. Option D is only direct selling, Option B requires single ownership of all channel levels, and Option C is a basic direct exchange between one seller and its buyers.

questions.question: A disagreement between a manufacturer and its own retailers over prices and margins is an example of
questions.explanation: Vertical conflict occurs between different levels of the same channel, such as a manufacturer and its retailers. Option D occurs between firms at the same level, such as two retailers of the same brand. Option C and Option A are types of channel cooperation, not conflict.

questions.question: The total volume of a product that would be bought by a defined customer group, in a defined geographical area, in a defined time period, in a defined marketing environment and under a defined marketing programme is called
questions.explanation: Market demand is the total amount all buyers in a defined group and area would buy in a given period under given conditions. Option D is only one company's share of that demand, Option A is a sales target set for a salesperson or territory, and Option C is a percentage, not a volume.

questions.question: Market potential is best defined as

options.a: the sales a company actually achieved in the last period
options.b: the level of sales that would occur with no marketing expenditure at all
options.c: a single company's expected sales under its chosen marketing plan
options.d: the limit approached by market demand as industry marketing expenditure approaches infinity, for a given marketing environment

questions.explanation: Market potential is the upper limit that total market demand approaches as industry marketing effort becomes very large in a given environment. Option B is the market minimum, Option A is past company sales, and Option C is the company sales forecast.

questions.question: The sales level of a product that would occur even without any marketing expenditure to stimulate demand is called the
questions.explanation: The market minimum is the baseline volume that would be bought with zero marketing spending. Option A is the ceiling reached as marketing spending becomes very large, Option B is the ceiling for one company, and Option D is a target set for the sales force.

questions.question: A company's estimated share of market demand at alternative levels of its marketing effort in a given time period is known as
questions.explanation: Company demand is the firm's share of total market demand, and it depends on how its marketing effort compares with competitors'. Option C and Option D refer to the whole market, not one company, and Option A is demand for the product category as a whole.

questions.question: The expected level of company sales based on a chosen marketing plan and an assumed marketing environment is called the
questions.explanation: A sales forecast is the firm's expected sales given the specific plan it has chosen and the environment it assumes. Option B is the maximum the company could reach if its marketing effort increased relative to competitors, while Option C and Option D refer to the whole market.

questions.question: What is the key difference between company sales potential and the company sales forecast?

options.a: There is no difference; the two terms mean exactly the same thing
options.b: Sales potential is always lower than the sales forecast
options.c: Sales potential refers to the whole industry, while the forecast refers to a single customer
options.d: Sales potential is the limit the company's sales could approach as its marketing effort increases relative to competitors, while the forecast is the sales expected under the plan actually chosen

questions.explanation: Company sales potential is a ceiling that the firm could approach with increasing marketing effort, while the forecast is the realistic expectation under its chosen plan. Option B is wrong because the forecast is normally at or below the potential. Option C confuses the levels of measurement, and Option A ignores the clear difference.

questions.question: A firm's sales expressed as a percentage of the total sales of all firms in the same market during the same period is the firm's
questions.explanation: Market share compares the firm's sales with total market sales. Option C is the theoretical ceiling for the whole market, Option B is a sales target, and Option A compares current market demand with potential demand rather than the firm with its rivals.

questions.question: A campaign that encourages more Nigerians to drink bottled water in general, rather than any particular brand, is trying to stimulate
questions.explanation: Primary demand is demand for the product category as a whole. Selective demand, Option D, is demand for a particular brand. Option A concerns one firm's share, and Option C is the level of sales with no marketing at all.

questions.question: A survey of buyers' intentions is MOST useful for forecasting when

options.a: buyers are few, can be reached cheaply, have clear intentions and are likely to carry them out
options.b: buyers are unwilling to share information about their plans
options.c: buyers are millions of scattered consumers who rarely plan purchases
options.d: the product is completely new and buyers cannot describe it

questions.explanation: Buyer-intention surveys work best when the buyers are few, the cost of reaching them is low, and they have clear intentions that they will carry out and are willing to disclose, as is common in industrial markets. Option C, Option D and Option B describe situations where stated intentions would be unreliable or hard to obtain.

questions.question: A forecasting method in which each salesperson estimates the likely sales in his or her territory and the estimates are added up (and adjusted by management) to give a company forecast is called

options.d: the sales-force composite (composite of sales-force opinions)

questions.explanation: The sales-force composite builds the forecast from the estimates of the people closest to customers. Option A uses a panel of experts in anonymous rounds, Option B sells the product in a test area, and Option C averages past sales figures.

questions.question: Which of the following is a well-known weakness of the sales-force composite method of forecasting?

options.a: Salespeople may be biased, for example deliberately underestimating so that their sales quotas are set low
options.b: It relies only on mathematical analysis of past sales
options.c: It cannot be broken down by territory or product
options.d: It ignores people who have direct contact with customers

questions.explanation: Sales representatives may be naturally optimistic or pessimistic, and some underestimate so that the company sets low quotas, so management usually adjusts their figures. Option C is wrong because the method gives estimates broken down by territory and product. Option B describes time-series analysis, and Option D is the opposite of the method.
